• Understand the purpose of HTML in web development

• Know the structure of a basic HTML document

• Identify common HTML elements and their roles

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Dr. Maya Patel. Today we’ll explore what HTML is and why it’s the building block of every website.

First, HTML gives structure to web pages—think of it as the skeleton that holds everything together. By the end of this session you’ll understand its purpose, see the anatomy of a basic HTML document, and recognize the most common elements and what they do.
Let’s start with the purpose: HTML tells browsers how to display text, images, and links. It’s the language that turns plain text into a web page you can interact with.
Next, a simple HTML document begins with <!DOCTYPE html>, followed by <html>, <head>, and <body> tags. These sections organize metadata, styles, and the visible content.

Finally, common elements like

for headings,

for paragraphs, and for links each have specific roles. Recognizing these will help you build and read web pages quickly.

Next, we have the essential tags: <html> wraps everything, <head> contains metadata like the <title>, and <body> holds the content you see on the page. Here’s a minimal example that displays ‘Hello World’.

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's dive into Links and Images, an essential part of building web pages.
First, the <a href="url"> tag creates a clickable link. When a user clicks the highlighted text, the browser navigates to the address you specify.
Next, the tag embeds an image. The src attribute points to the image file, and the alt attribute provides a text description for accessibility.
Remember, always include meaningful alt text so screen readers can describe the image to users who can’t see it.
To summarize, use the anchor tag for links, the img tag for pictures, and never forget descriptive alt text. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• Ordered lists (<ol>) vs. unordered lists (<ul>)

• Table basics: <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td>

• Form essentials: <form>, <input>, <label>, <textarea>, <button>

actions.text: Welcome, everyone. I’m Dr. Maya Patel. Today we’ll quickly review three core HTML structures: lists, tables, and forms.

First, let’s talk about lists. An ordered list (<ol>) numbers each item, while an unordered list (<ul>) uses bullet points. For example, a recipe step‑by‑step would use <ol>, whereas a shopping list works well with <ul>.

Next, tables provide a grid layout with rows and columns. The basic tags are <table> for the container, <tr> for each row, <th> for header cells, and <td> for data cells. Think of a simple schedule: each day is a column header, and each time slot is a row.

Finally, forms let users submit information. The key elements are <form> to wrap everything, <input> for single‑line data, <label> to describe each field, <textarea> for multi‑line text, and <button> to trigger submission. Imagine a contact page where you enter your name, email, and message.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to create a level 2 heading?
questions.analysis: The <h2> tag defines a level‑2 heading. <heading> is not a valid HTML tag, <title> belongs in the <head> section, and <head> contains metadata, not visible headings.

questions.question: Which element creates a hyperlink to another webpage?
questions.analysis: The <a> (anchor) element is used for hyperlinks, with the href attribute specifying the target URL. <link> is for external resources like stylesheets, while <href> and <url> are not standalone tags.

elements.content:
• Use semantic tags: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Provide meaningful headings and descriptive alt attributes

• Indent code and keep structure tidy

actions.text: Alright, let’s dive into Semantic HTML and best practices. Using the right tags helps both people and browsers understand our page structure.
First, we’ll focus on semantic tags like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer>. These describe the purpose of each part of the page.
Here’s a quick example showing a header containing a navigation menu, followed by the main content and a footer. Notice how the tags clearly label each section.
Remember to add meaningful headings and alt attributes to images—this makes your site accessible to screen readers.
Finally, keep your code indented and tidy; a clean structure is easier to read and maintain. Any questions before we move on?

questions.question: Which HTML tag is most appropriate for the main heading of a webpage?
questions.analysis: The h1 element defines the top-level heading of the page content. The title element belongs in the head and is not displayed in the body. Header is a sectioning element that can contain headings but is not itself a heading. Div is a generic container.

questions.question: Which group of tags best represents the correct order of semantic sections for a typical article page?
questions.analysis: A well‑structured page starts with a header (site title/logo), followed by navigation, then the main content, and ends with a footer. The other options place elements in illogical order or omit required sections.

questions.analysis: In option D the opening tag is h1 but the closing tag is h2, creating mismatched heading tags. All other snippets are correctly nested and closed.
